This site is a Drupal site. There is no Drupal running behind it.

Everything you are reading was rendered by Nuxt at build time, from a Drupal that existed for the length of that build and was then thrown away. The pages are static files on GitHub Pages. When somebody wants to write, a Drupal is started on demand, held open for as long as they need it, and destroyed again.

Why bother

A small Drupal site spends almost all of its life idle and all of its life being a server: patched, backed up, watched, and paid for. The reason it has to be up is that a visitor might arrive, and Drupal decides what a visitor sees.

Decoupling moves that decision to build time. Druxt reads Drupal over JSON:API and Nuxt renders the result to files, so what a visitor sees is decided once, when the site is built. After that, Drupal is only needed by the person writing.

That is the whole idea. The rest is arranging for Drupal to be there when somebody writes, and gone when nobody is.

The three pieces

  • Drupal, with its content and configuration committed to the repository by Tome. It is installed from those files, used, and deleted.
  • Nuxt with Druxt, which reads Drupal over JSON:API and builds the static site.
  • GitHub Actions, which builds and deploys, and which can stand a Drupal up on request.

Nothing here is persistent except the repository. The database is created from committed files every time, which means the repository is the site: clone it and you have everything, including the content.

Build it yourself

The starter kit installs the frontend, Composer, and a local Drupal 11 on SQLite, straight from committed config and content:

npx giget@1 gh:druxt/quickstart-druxt-serverless#develop my-site --install
cd my-site
npm run generate

It needs PHP 8.3 or newer and Composer. The install provisions Drupal, starts it, and leaves you with a backend on 127.0.0.1:8888 and a static build in nuxt/dist.

Point a browser at nuxt/dist and stop Drupal. The site keeps working, because nothing it serves needed Drupal after the build:

cd drupal && ./.devtools/stop
npx serve -s nuxt/dist

Deploying to Pages

The deploy workflow does what the install did, then publishes what it built. The Drupal it provisions lives and dies inside the job:

- name: Provision Drupal
  working-directory: drupal
  run: |
    .devtools/assemble
    .devtools/provision
    .devtools/start

- name: Generate the static site
  working-directory: nuxt
  env:
    ROUTER_BASE: /
    CONTENT_REPOSITORY: ${{ github.repository }}
  run: npm run generate

A user site at <name>.github.io serves from the domain root and needs no base path. A project site needs ROUTER_BASE: /<repo>/, because a static build bakes its asset paths in.

Editing it

Turn on Edit and every entity on the page gains a control. This is the frontend's own editing layer, not Drupal's: the site is static, and what you change is held in the browser.

Changes go into a cart. They are held in the browser, they survive a reload, and nothing is written until you say so. The page renders them as you type, so the site reads the way it will read once the change is merged rather than showing you a badge and asking you to imagine it.

Preview shows a change as the site will render it, in whichever view mode you ask for and at a real device width. The widths are real rather than a zoom, so the site's own media queries decide the layout. A page wider than the window is scaled down to fit, and the scale is a control.

Sending the work

There are two destinations, and they answer different questions.

Commit to backend sends the cart to a running Drupal over JSON:API, one request per resource, in dependency order. This is the short loop, and it validates against the site's real field definitions.

Open a pull request needs no backend at all. The cart becomes a document in a branch: the JSON:API resources, the bytes of any picture, and an explicit list of deletions. A job on that pull request stands a Drupal up, applies the document through the entity API, and commits back the content Tome writes, so review sees the real content diff rather than a description of one.

The conversion happens in Drupal on purpose. Tome writes Drupal's own normalisation: references by target_uuid, an image's width and height read off the file, the processed body. Reproducing that in JavaScript means keeping a copy of Drupal's normalisers in step with a Drupal that moves, which fails quietly and produces pull requests that review cleanly and break the next build.

Starting a backend

When you do want Drupal, a workflow starts one. It provisions the site, exposes it through a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel, publishes where it is, and holds it open:

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      minutes:
        description: 'How long to hold the backend open'
        default: '55'

workflow_dispatch is restricted to people with write access to the repository, which is the access control the whole thing rests on. There is no other way to start a session, and no push, pull request or schedule can.

The session publishes its address to a branch, and the frontend reads it. When the job ends, the tunnel closes and the record is deleted. Nothing is left running.

What it costs you

Honestly, some things are worse this way.

  • Publishing is a build. Content is live when the site rebuilds, not when you press save. For a site that publishes a few times a week that is fine. For a newsroom it is not.
  • Anything Drupal does per request is gone. Personalisation, forms that write on submit, anything reading the current user. What is left is what can be decided at build time.
  • Starting a backend takes a few minutes. Provisioning Drupal from scratch is not instant, and you wait for it.

What you get back is a site with no server to keep up, no database to back up, no security releases to chase on a schedule somebody else sets, and a full copy of everything in one repository.

The code is at druxt/quickstart-druxt-serverless, and this site is at Decipher/Decipher.github.io.
